title: VAR has become too ‘microscopic’, says UEFA head of refereeing
content:
Roberto Rosetti, UEFA’s head of refereeing, believes VAR has become too “microscopic” and claims the reason for the technology’s introduction in the first place has been forgotten.

The 58-year-old, a former Serie A referee who has headed up UEFA’s refereeing department since 2018, oversees the officiating in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League.

“About the VAR intervention, I can tell you this: I believe that we forgot the reason why VAR was introduced,” the Italian said. “We forgot a little bit. Everywhere. You remember, eight years ago, I came to London. We discussed the ‘what VAR stands for’. We spoke about clear mistakes.

“Why we spoke about clear and obvious mistakes. Because technology works so well in factual decisions. In objective decisions, it is fantastic. For interpretations, subjective evaluation is more difficult. That’s why we started to speak about clear and obvious mistakes — clear evidence.

“I believe that we need to, at the end of the season, again in our meetings, to speak about this. We cannot go in this direction of microscopic VAR intervention. We love football like it is.”

Asked to expand on what he meant by VAR becoming too “microscopic”, Rosetti made reference to a 1920s film editing machine.

“We call this moviola,” the Italian added. “Have you ever heard this word? It is this: when you are watching the situation with the super slow motion, you can find a lot of things.”

Rosetti would not be drawn on comparing UEFA’s and the Premier League’s implementation of VAR, saying he “wouldn’t be happy” if Howard Webb — head of the Professional Game Match Officials Board — spoke about their situations.

“It’s a matter of respect with my big friend,” Rosetti said. “I don’t want to touch.”

However, what Rosetti did do during his media briefing in Brussels on Thursday, where he talked reporters through several refereeing decisions, was detail how in the Champions League this season there have been 0.36 on-field reviews per match.

This is the highest it has been since VAR was introduced to the competition in 2019-20 and double the number of on-field reviews per match when compared to 2021-22.

The Premier League has a much lower rate of on-field reviews, 0.15 per match, which is less than half of the men’s Champions League average.

When asked if VAR has now gone too far, and subsequently how it can be improved across the board, Rosetti said the media has played a role in how it is being used.

“You said this, not me,” he added. “You are guilty in some way, because also you pushed for more interventions. Where is VAR? Why VAR doesn’t intervene? Why VAR is not involved? What are the VARs doing?

“But now we need to be careful about that. It can improve by speaking — to meet and fix.”
